He asks the trainer to run the same hand motion twice at half speed, then signs the assessor sheet beside the exact step that broke.
examples.whatToDo: Mark the frozen step and repeat that exact sequence slowly under observation. Do not protect the embarrassed hand from the drill it needs.
examples.whyItMatters: Avoiding the switch would make humiliation the new instructor. Repeating the step turns public failure into a precise return point.

examples.title: Adrian Logs the Lap Count
examples.scenario: A lane rope drips onto a laminated rehab lane sheet after Adrian climbs out of the pool on Wednesday night. His shoulder pain ended the heat in front of everyone. He has to decide whether to call the season cursed or stop before the spike, log the exact lap count, and return at 6:00 a.m. for kick-only work. He writes the first pain-free lap time on the rehab sheet, circles the stroke that held, and leaves before pride turns the drill into a race.
examples.whatToDo: Stop before the pain spike, record the lap count, and come back for the controlled kick set. Do not use shame as a season-ending diagnosis.
examples.whyItMatters: The log separates real pain from the story that the pool is now forbidden. Kick-only work keeps contact without pretending the shoulder is fine.

examples.title: Giulia Names the Butter Break
examples.scenario: "The layers are gone," Giulia says, cutting open a split croissant on the steel bench at 4:30 p.m. Butter has pooled where the sheet broke. The chef says nothing, hand on the bench scraper. Giulia must decide whether to clear the tray fast or name the butter break and roll one new test block under his quiet count. She saves the split batch in a clear tub, labels the fold where the butter broke, and asks for one slower turn before starting a new tray.
examples.whatToDo: Cut the failed piece open, name the break, and roll one test block slowly. Keep the failure on the bench until it teaches the hand.
examples.whyItMatters: Hiding the tray would protect embarrassment. The test block returns to the exact failed layer while the correction is still visible.

examples.title: Saul Rewinds the Radio Report
examples.scenario: A training handset lies beside Derek's crumpled run sheet in the ambulance bay after evaluation. His voice cracked on the radio report, and the missing blood pressure line is circled in blue. Derek has to choose whether to joke about nerves or rewind the recording, write the line, and repeat the report until the sequence holds. Derek copies the missing blood-pressure line onto the next run sheet, rehearses the radio report aloud, and refuses to call the crack in his voice the whole story.
examples.whatToDo: Rewind the recording, write the missing line, and repeat the report into the handset until the order stays intact.
examples.whyItMatters: The cracked voice exposed the pressure point. Repeating the exact radio sequence builds armor where the evaluation actually hit.

examples.title: Benoit Reheats the Small Gather
examples.scenario: A green glass shard catches light on Benoit's steel bench after the buyer leaves. The temperature log shows the drop he wanted to ignore. He places the shard beside the annealing shelf, notes the number, and reheats a small gather instead of starting a showpiece that would let pride pretend nothing cracked. He tapes the temperature number to the annealing shelf, repeats one smaller pour, and waits for the glass to cool before judging the day.
examples.whatToDo: Keep the shard on the bench, note the temperature drop, and reheat a small gather. Return to the cause at a controllable size.
examples.whyItMatters: The showpiece would turn repair into ego protection. The small gather tests the exposed failure without hiding from the buyer's rejection.

questions.prompt: A trainer says a setback becomes useful only when the return drill touches the exact point that failed. What is the main idea?
choices: Durability is built through accurate return, not denial or dramatic proof.
Setbacks should be repeated until they stop hurting.
The best response to failure is always a smaller version of the same task.
questions.explanation: The important piece is accurate, controlled contact with the exposed point. Repeating pain for its own sake is denial, and not every return is simply a smaller duplicate.

questions.prompt: A violinist strains her wrist and wants to prove she is back by playing the hardest passage. Her rehab sheet calls for slow open-string work. What should she do?
choices: Play the hard passage once to rebuild confidence.
Follow the slow rehab pattern and stop at the prescribed dose.
Avoid the instrument until the fear disappears.
questions.explanation: The slow pattern returns to the skill without letting pride set the dose. The hard passage risks turning proof into injury, while avoidance lets fear claim the instrument.

questions.prompt: An electrician freezes during a simulation and wants a different drill next week so the crew forgets. What is the better response?
choices: Let him switch drills so confidence can rebuild gradually.
Have him watch a senior electrician perform it until it feels normal.
Mark the frozen step and repeat that sequence slowly with the assessor present.
questions.explanation: The frozen step is the map. Repeating it slowly trains the exposed point, while switching drills or only watching protects him from the exact place that needs work.

questions.prompt: A swimmer leaves a heat with shoulder pain and wants to quit the season because the pool now feels humiliating. Which plan fits best?
choices: Log the lap count, stop before the spike, and return for kick-only work.
Swim the next heat hard so teammates know he is not afraid.
Stay away from the pool until the shame has fully passed.
questions.explanation: The lap log and kick-only return separate real pain from a verdict on the season. Proving courage risks damage, while staying away lets shame define the pool.

questions.prompt: A pastry apprentice ruins laminated dough and wants to throw out the tray before anyone sees. What should the chef ask her to do?
choices: Start a fresh batch immediately so she does not dwell on the failure.
Cut the failed piece open, name the butter break, and roll one test block slowly.
Leave the kitchen for ten minutes to calm down.
questions.explanation: The cut-open piece makes the failure teach the next roll. Starting fresh too fast hides the cause, and calming down alone does not train the lamination step.

questions.prompt: In a bakery prep kitchen after a collapsed laminated dough test, a trainee wants to dump the batch and stay late making a fresh one. The chef asks for one repair before the next fold. Which response uses controlled failure best?
choices: It ignores the fact that most radio reports are easy after enough time.
It focuses too much on the missing information and not enough on confidence.
It turns one exposed sequence into a permanent identity instead of a drill target.
questions.explanation: The missed sequence should become practice material, not identity. Ease and confidence are secondary; the exact pressure point is what must be trained.

questions.prompt: A coach tells an injured athlete, 'Real toughness means acting like it never happened.' What is the problem with that advice?
choices: It confuses armor with numbness and may hide the exact return protocol needed.
It is too harsh because athletes should avoid discomfort after injury.
It makes competition less emotional than it should be.
questions.explanation: Pretending nothing happened skips the accurate return. The issue is not avoiding all discomfort or preserving emotion, but training the exposed point honestly.

questions.prompt: A glassblower starts a showpiece right after a cracked commission because he wants the buyer's rejection out of his head. Why is a small gather stronger?
choices: It is easier, so it avoids negative emotion.
It targets the temperature error without letting pride choose the scale.
It proves that buyers do not understand craft standards.
questions.explanation: The small gather returns to the cause at a controllable size. Avoiding emotion is not the aim, and blaming buyers would protect the ego from the temperature log.

questions.prompt: Two athletes suffer setbacks. One designs a careful return drill. The other gives a speech about being unbreakable and skips rehab limits. Which response is stronger?
choices: The speech, because belief speeds recovery.
They are equal if both athletes care deeply.
The return drill, because it builds contact with the exposed point without lying about risk.
questions.explanation: The drill is stronger because it respects the setback and trains the precise point of failure. The speech may feel bold, but skipping limits can become fake invulnerability.

reviewCards.front: A setback exposes one weak point. What should the first return drill touch?
reviewCards.back: It should touch the exact exposed point at a controlled dose. Avoidance leaves fear in charge, while dramatic proof may create a second injury.

reviewCards.front: Why is numbness a weak version of mental armor?
reviewCards.back: Numbness hides feedback. Real armor uses the feedback to design a return that is honest, repeatable, and close enough to train the damaged spot.

reviewCards.front: A person wants a grand comeback after humiliation. What should you look for instead?
reviewCards.back: Look for the smallest return that directly trains the point of failure. Grand proof often protects pride; small accurate practice builds the next layer.

reviewCards.front: How can a painful failure become a map instead of a verdict?
reviewCards.back: Mark where the failure happened, then build a drill at that location. The exposed spot tells you where to return, not who you permanently are.

reviewCards.front: When does pushing through pain become the wrong move?
reviewCards.back: It becomes wrong when the push ignores the return protocol and turns pride into the coach. Accurate contact matters more than looking fearless.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to build durability through accurate return. The skill is naming the point a setback exposed, then touching it again at a dose that trains rather than denies.

ifThenPlans.plan: If injury tempts you to prove you are back, then follow the smallest prescribed return before attempting the impressive task.
If you freeze under observation, then mark the exact step and repeat only that sequence slowly with a witness.
If a failed piece embarrasses you, then keep the failed part visible while you make one small corrected test.
If your voice cracks in a report or presentation, then replay the line and rehearse that sequence before changing topics.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Choose one setback you keep avoiding. Build a return drill that touches the exact failed point for less than ten minutes today.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: At week's end, list every place you avoided because it carried shame. Pick one and schedule a controlled return with a clear stopping rule.
